column5: Evening and morning form one day
column6: The commentary joins night to day as parts of time; Genesis names light day and darkness night, then closes the first day with evening and morning, giving the pair an ordered whole.

column5: Day/night and winter/summer succession
column6: The commentary links successive days with winter's appointed interval; the promise that seedtime, harvest, cold, heat, summer, winter, day, and night will not cease makes those alternating parts a stable covenantal rhythm.

column5: Day speaks to day, night to night
column6: The commentary pictures adjoining periods as a chain; the psalm has each day pour speech into the next and each night disclose knowledge to the next, making succession itself communicative.

column5: Day and night belong to God
column6: The commentary treats the paired periods as more than an undifferentiated flow; the psalm addresses God as owner of both day and night and maker of the luminaries that mark them.

column5: Summer and winter formed by God
column6: The commentary moves from daily pairs to winter's middle and cold; this verse attributes the formation of summer and winter, as well as earth's bounds, to God.

column5: An appointed time for every affair
column6: The commentary calls time a sequence of distinct intervals; Ecclesiastes introduces its paired occasions by assigning each affair its own time under heaven.

column5: Birth and death have their times
column6: The commentary develops youth, age, and the end of life; this pair places birth and death at separate appointed moments rather than treating a life as a single span.

column5: A thousand years like yesterday
column6: The commentary says a long lifetime shrinks to an evening or a daytime hour when viewed at the end; the psalm compares a thousand years before God to yesterday once passed and to a night watch.

column5: Humans are of yesterday
column6: The commentary puts human life inside a vast time before one existed; Bildad says humans are only of yesterday and know little because their earthly days are a shadow.

column5: Number days to gain wisdom
column6: The commentary makes the countable stages of a life matter for righteous action; the psalm asks God to teach humans to count their days so that they acquire a wise heart.

column5: My times are in your hand
column6: The commentary places the pieces and limits of a person's life under God's ordering; the psalmist entrusts his own times to God's hand while asking deliverance from enemies.

column5: Days written before any existed
column6: The commentary juxtaposes a long time before human existence with life's later stages; the psalm says the speaker's days were recorded when none of them had yet come, placing the life course in divine foreknowledge.

column5: Remember the creator in youth
column6: The commentary names youth as one interval of a finite life; Ecclesiastes commands remembrance specifically in youthful days before difficult later years arrive.

column5: Old age and the next generation
column6: The commentary joins successive life stages to people sustaining one another; the aged speaker asks not to be forsaken until he tells the next generation of God's power.

column5: Even a century is a small life span
column6: The commentary counts human ages and then reduces a whole life to a brief interval; Sirach calls a hundred years a large number of human days before measuring them against eternity.

column5: Few years beside eternal days
column6: The commentary says lengthy human residence looks like only a small daytime fraction; Sirach likens human years against eternity to a drop of sea water or a grain of sand.

column5: The impious claim death returns them to nonexistence
column6: The commentary recalls the claim that time alone destroys and counters it with final reckoning; Wisdom puts in the impious speakers' mouths the claim that chance brought them into being and afterward they will be as though they had never existed.

column5: Life as a passing shadow
column6: The commentary says the long stay contracts to an evening or an hour; the impious speakers in Wisdom compare life to a passing shadow, though the book presents their conclusion about death as mistaken.

column5: Truth taught while waiting all day
column6: The commentary places counsel in truth and patience inside the day's span; the psalmist asks to be taught God's truth and says he waits for God all day.

column5: Appointed vision, waiting through delay
column6: The commentary binds patience to a true promise whose fulfillment has its own time; the vision points to its appointed end and the hearer must wait even if it seems delayed.

column5: Blessed one who waits through counted days
column6: The commentary makes endurance stretch over a measured interval; Daniel blesses the person who waits to the specified day count, joining a finite duration to perseverance.

column5: Torah meditated day and night
column6: The commentary sets truth-oriented persistence across the two periods; the righteous person's meditation on the Torah fills both day and night.

column5: Day-night instruction becomes action
column6: The commentary joins right deeds to a time-spanning attachment to truth; Joshua must meditate on the book of Torah day and night so that he acts according to it.

column5: Teach others at lying down and rising
column6: The commentary says people become linked through repeated counsel while time passes; Israel is to teach the words to children while sitting, walking, lying down, and rising.

column5: Morning instruction sustains the weary
column6: The commentary has people uphold one another through truth across successive mornings; the servant receives an awakened ear morning by morning so he can sustain the weary with a word.

column5: The God-fearing speak to one another
column6: The commentary depicts the surviving group as people bound by reciprocal exhortation; those who fear God speak together, and God attends to them and records their remembrance.

column5: Speak truth to one's neighbor
column6: The commentary's mutual counsel is specifically counsel in truth; Zechariah commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor and to render truthful, peace-making judgments.

column5: One group urges another to seek God
column6: The commentary's people attach themselves to one another through counsel; the city's inhabitants invite others to go entreat God and add that they themselves will go.

column5: Accumulation and ignorance of its heir
column6: The commentary recalls the preceding surah's race to multiply possessions until death; the psalm says a person heaps wealth without knowing who will gather it after him. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, but this row rests on the developed accumulation motif, not a claimed shared meaning with patience.

column5: Winter labor and later want
column6: The commentary gives winter's cold a place in patient seasonal time; the sluggard refuses to plow in winter and therefore seeks food at harvest without finding it, showing how one interval governs the next.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: fixed life limit
column6: The table offers a sound correspondence only, not proven cognacy; Job says a human's days and months are determined and God set a חק, a limit he cannot pass, a specific counterpart to the commentary's allotted life stages and due times.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: prescribed light cycles
column6: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; Jeremiah calls the sun for daylight and the moon and stars for night divinely established ordinances, connecting the commentary's linked periods to a prescribed cosmic order.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: enduring ordinances
column6: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; the continued existence of Israel is made contingent on those day-night ordinances departing, linking regular time to the survival of a people.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: inscribed light-dark boundary
column6: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Job describes a marked circle on the waters at the boundary of light and darkness, giving the commentary's adjoining night and day a sharply marked boundary.

column5: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: eighth-day assembly
column6: The table gives a sound correspondence, not a proven cognate of time; after seven days of offerings this verse prescribes an eighth-day עצרת, where successive counted days culminate in people assembling.

column5: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: seventh-day assembly
column6: The table's sound correspondence alone does not establish cognacy; after six days of unleavened bread the seventh is an עצרת, joining a counted sequence to communal gathering as in the commentary's meeting of time and people.

column5: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: daily reading, eighth-day assembly
column6: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Ezra reads the Torah day by day through the festival, then the people hold an eighth-day עצרת, making repeated instruction and a final joined assembly one timed practice.

column5: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: call an assembly
column6: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; the command to blow the trumpet, sanctify a fast, and call an עצרה gives the commentary's people joined through urgent exhortation a concrete communal form.

column5: Every age gathers together
column6: The commentary names stages of life before showing people joined; Joel's summoned gathering explicitly includes elders, children, nursing infants, bridegroom, and bride.

column5: Assembly joined to injustice is rejected
column6: The commentary makes righteous deeds and truth conditions of collective survival; Isaiah refuses an assembly held together with wrongdoing, testing the value of a gathered religious community by its conduct. Hebrew עצרה is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r, without proof of cognacy.

column5: Endurance until the end
column6: The commentary says those who endure remain through the chain of time; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, making persistence across the whole interval decisive.

column5: Stored years collapse into one night
column6: The commentary contrasts a lifetime of numerical accumulation with its abrupt end; the rich man's planned many years are cut short that very night, and he is asked who will have his stored goods.

column5: Possessions imagined to guarantee many years
column6: The commentary links the competition to increase possessions with failure to notice time passing; the rich man addresses his soul as though stored goods secured many years of rest.

column5: Enlarged barns for accumulated goods
column6: The commentary recalls multiplying wealth until the grave; the rich man decides to build larger barns to store all his grain and goods before his mortality is exposed in the story.

column5: Life appears briefly and vanishes
column6: The commentary reduces a seeming long residence to a small interval; James calls human life a vapor that appears a little while and disappears, addressing people who plan future years.

column5: One day and a thousand years
column6: The commentary contrasts long duration with its apparent contraction; this verse reversibly compares one day and a thousand years before the Lord, relativizing ordinary measures of waiting.

column5: Delayed promise and divine patience
column6: The commentary connects patience to the true promise through a shrinking lifetime; this verse says the promised coming is not slow as some reckon but delayed in divine patience to allow repentance.

column5: Appointed periods for human peoples
column6: The commentary divides time into assigned intervals while people remain joined; Paul says God made every nation from one and determined their appointed times and dwelling boundaries.

column5: The remaining time is shortened
column6: The commentary says a long life is seen as compressed when its end approaches; Paul tells believers the appointed time has grown short and therefore their ordinary life relations must be held lightly.

column5: Outer decline, daily inner renewal
column6: The commentary tracks bodily life through aging while patience persists across days; Paul says the outer person wastes away but the inner person is renewed day by day.

column5: Exhort one another every day
column6: The commentary's people remain joined through reciprocal counsel across linked days; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation while it is called Today, to prevent hardening through sin.

column5: Stir one another to good works
column6: The commentary makes shared righteous action part of how people remain connected; Hebrews asks believers to consider one another so as to provoke love and good deeds.

column5: Gather and encourage as the Day approaches
column6: The commentary connects communal exhortation to passing time; Hebrews opposes abandoning assembly and urges increasingly mutual encouragement as the approaching Day is seen.

column5: Three years of night-and-day admonition
column6: The commentary ties mutual counsel to morning/evening and a lasting interval; Paul recalls three years in which he warned each person night and day with tears.

column5: Exhort at every season with patience
column6: The commentary's counsel and patience fill successive times; the charge to proclaim the word in season and out of season includes correction and exhortation with complete patience and teaching.

column5: Good action sustained until its season
column6: The commentary joins righteous deeds and patience across time; Paul says not to grow weary in doing good because a harvest will come at its proper time if people do not give up.

column5: Night is advanced, day draws near
column6: The commentary makes night-to-day transition a call to moral action; Paul says the passing night and approaching day demand casting off dark works and taking up the armor of light.

column5: Work during the remaining day
column6: The commentary links right deeds to the short allotted interval; Jesus says the works of the sender must be done while it is day, since night comes when no one can work.

column5: Use the time because days are evil
column6: The commentary makes limited time the setting for righteous action; Ephesians asks its hearers to make the most of the time because the days are evil.

column5: Elect cry day and night for justice
column6: The commentary places truth and patient appeal across daily cycles; Jesus describes God's chosen crying to him day and night for justice in a parable about persistent prayer.

column5: The slain ask how long until judgment
column6: The commentary connects waiting with a true final reckoning; the slain ask the sovereign Lord how long before he judges and vindicates their blood.

column5: Rest a little longer until number complete
column6: The commentary gives patient waiting a finite interval and links the fates of people; the martyrs are told to rest a little longer until their fellow servants are complete.

column5: Endurance, divine commands, and faith
column6: The commentary's surviving group combines belief, deeds, and patience; Revelation characterizes the saints' endurance by keeping God's commandments and faith in Jesus.

column5: Speaking truth together builds maturity
column6: The commentary makes counsel in truth a way people are joined; speaking truth in love is the means by which members grow toward their common head, Christ.

column5: The body joined by every working part
column6: The commentary says the people who remain are added to one another; the body is joined and held together as each part works, building itself up in love.

column5: Encourage and build one another
column6: The commentary's repeated reciprocal counsel makes a durable community; Paul explicitly tells believers to encourage one another and build one another up.

column5: Admonish, help, and be patient with all
column6: The commentary couples mutual counsel with patience; this instruction names admonishing the idle, helping the weak, and being patient with everyone as communal practices.

column5: Winter intensifies the coming ordeal
column6: The commentary names winter's hard cold as one temporal condition for patience; Jesus tells hearers to pray that their flight does not occur in winter, when that season will worsen their urgent journey.

column5: Morning mercy and nightly faithfulness
column6: The commentary pairs morning and evening as recurring occasions for patient devotion; the sabbath psalm assigns proclamation of God's kindness to morning and his faithfulness to nights.

column5: Remember God at night and keep law
column6: The commentary has enduring adherence to truth through the nighttime portion; the psalmist remembers God's name at night and keeps his law.

column5: Wake through night watches for instruction
column6: The commentary makes patient fidelity stretch across night and morning; the psalmist's eyes anticipate the watches of the night to meditate on God's saying.

column5: Evening, morning, noon prayer
column6: The commentary explicitly pairs morning with late day; the psalmist names evening, morning, and noon as repeated times of appeal to God, dividing the day into acts of persistence.

column5: Daytime care and nighttime song
column6: The commentary makes night and day adjoining parts of a lived religious interval; the psalmist expects God's kindness by day and a song-prayer with him at night.

column5: Human cannot grasp time's whole work
column6: The commentary says the connected pieces are more than a flat flow; Ecclesiastes says God made each thing fitting in its time while humans cannot discover the work from beginning to end.

column5: Old age approaches the lasting home
column6: The commentary takes youth through decline to the grave; Ecclesiastes' portrait of the aging person's fears ends with going to the lasting home while mourners walk outside.

column5: Seventy or eighty years pass quickly
column6: The commentary catalogs life stages but says all that time can contract at the end; the psalm gives a human span of seventy or eighty years and says it quickly passes.

column5: Infant and elder days transformed
column6: The commentary counts childhood and old age among life's parts; Isaiah's promised city reverses premature death, saying infants will not live only a few days and elders will complete their days.

column5: As though never existing, womb to grave
column6: The commentary recalls a time when a human was not yet a mentioned thing and a later journey to death; Job wishes he had been as though he had not existed, carried directly from womb to grave.

column5: Days as a passing shadow
column6: The commentary compresses lifetime into a brief seeming stay; the psalm says human days resemble a shadow that passes away.

column5: Human lifetime as grass
column6: The commentary's phases of life culminate in disappearance; the psalm compares mortal days to grass flourishing briefly as a flower of the field.

column5: A passing wind erases its place
column6: The commentary asks how much of a long life remains at its end; when wind passes over the flower it is gone and its place knows it no more, the next part of the mortal image.

column5: Winter has passed
column6: The commentary calls winter a particular hard interval and ties waiting to its end; the lover announces that winter and its rain are over, so the harsh season has a bounded duration.

column5: Ant stores food in summer and harvest
column6: The commentary connects accumulation to passing time; the ant gathers provisions in summer and at harvest, supplying a purposeful seasonal counterpart to accumulation that distracts humans until death.

column5: Wicked person piles silver
column6: The commentary recalls competitive increase of possessions before mortality; Job's wicked figure heaps silver like dust and clothing like clay, preparing the reversal in the next verse. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, not a demonstrated shared sense with patience.

column5: Another receives what was piled
column6: The commentary's hoarder cannot carry accumulated time or goods beyond life's end; Job says the righteous will wear the wicked person's prepared clothes and the innocent will divide his silver.

column5: Joseph heaps grain across good years
column6: The commentary recalls multiplying material stores before a later interval; Joseph piles grain beyond counting ahead of famine, giving accumulation a collective preserving purpose. Hebrew צבר is only the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r; the connection is the concrete stored-grain scene.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: day-night statutes
column6: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God's fixed ordinances of heaven and earth accompany his covenant with day and night, tying the commentary's alternating periods to continuing communal existence.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: heaven's ordinances
column6: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God asks Job whether he knows the ordinances of heaven or can establish their rule on earth, an interpretive bridge from the commentary's due times to cosmic prescription.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: assigned sea boundary
column6: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Wisdom recalls God setting the sea its prescribed limit, a spatial analogue to the commentary's precisely bounded intervals and seasonal middles.

column5: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: communal crisis assembly
column6: The table's sound correspondence does not prove cognacy; Joel calls a fast and an עצרה in which elders and all inhabitants gather at God's house and cry out, linking group survival to shared action in a hard time.

column5: Be still and wait despite evildoer success
column6: The commentary says patience must be sustained while truth is not yet manifest; the psalm tells its hearer to wait patiently for God rather than fret over a person succeeding in an evil course.

column5: Waiting renews strength
column6: The commentary treats patience as what lets people keep standing through a long interval; Isaiah says those waiting for God renew strength and continue without fainting.

column5: Quietly wait for salvation
column6: The commentary connects a difficult period with patient endurance; Lamentations calls quiet waiting for God's salvation good amid its account of suffering.

column5: Three daily prayers despite hostile decree
column6: The commentary stretches the act of patience between recurring times of day; Daniel continues praying three times daily even after the written decree against that practice.

column5: People hold onto another to go together
column6: The commentary says people are added to one another through a shared orientation to God; Zechariah imagines people of many languages grasping a Jew's garment and asking to go with him because God is with the group.

column5: One person sharpens another
column6: The commentary's reciprocal exhortation makes persons sustain one another; the proverb compares one person's effect on a friend to iron sharpening iron, giving counsel a mutual formative action.

column5: Named ages of a human life
column6: The commentary explicitly parses youth, maturity, and decline as time's pieces; Avot gives a sequence of ages with different pursuits and capacities, including forty for understanding and seventy for old age. Section numbering varies by edition.

column5: Acquire a friend and a teacher
column6: The commentary makes people remain linked by guidance; Avot directs a person to make a teacher and acquire a friend, turning endurance into a sustained interpersonal practice.

column5: If not now, when; if only for self, what am I
column6: The commentary binds short time to the need for others; Hillel's paired questions reject delay and self-enclosure in the same ethical saying.

column5: Do not defer study until free time
column6: The commentary says time is spent in successive limited pieces; Avot warns that a hoped-for leisure interval may never come, making present instruction urgent.

column5: Repent one day before death
column6: The commentary says a long life can shrink suddenly to its last fraction; the rabbinic explanation of repentance one day before death is to repent each day because no one knows which day will be last.

column5: Evening before morning in prayer order
column6: The commentary puts night and day into a deliberate sequence; the discussion explains beginning the daily Shema with evening by appealing to creation's evening followed by morning, turning Genesis' order into a repeated act.

column5: Prayer and fasting night and day
column6: The commentary places steadfast worship across the paired periods; the aged Anna serves in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day, joining old age with continuous devotion.

column5: Hope for unseen end requires patience
column6: The commentary asks people to wait through an interval for a promised resolution; Paul says those hoping for what they do not yet see wait for it with endurance.

column5: Endurance receives the promised thing
column6: The commentary joins patience to the true promise; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will so that hearers may receive what was promised.

column5: Divine patience counted as salvation
column6: The commentary joins the waiting interval to the chance to remain among the saved; Peter explicitly asks readers to regard the Lord's patience as salvation, supplying the purpose of the delay.

column5: Farmer waits through seasonal rains
column6: The commentary names winter's severity and the waiting that spans seasons; James asks believers to be patient like a farmer waiting for precious fruit through early and late rain until the Lord's coming.

column5: Prophets as examples of patient speech
column6: The commentary couples truth-telling with endurance; James names prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.

column5: Present opportunity used for good to all
column6: The commentary says righteous deeds and mutual support occupy limited time; Paul says that while opportunity remains believers should do good to everyone, especially fellow believers.

column5: Teach and admonish one another
column6: The commentary defines the surviving group through mutual counsel; Colossians asks believers to let Christ's word dwell among them as they teach and admonish one another wisely.

column5: Speak truth as members of one another
column6: The commentary brings truth and people being joined into one image; Ephesians gives membership in one body as the reason for each person to speak truth to a neighbor.

column5: Patient affliction with persistent prayer
column6: The commentary stretches patience between repeated times of worship; Paul joins patience in tribulation to constancy in prayer as the group's practice.

column5: Day of the Lord arrives during night
column6: The commentary juxtaposes the day-night pair with the sudden end of a seeming long stay; Paul says the Lord's day comes like a thief in the night, challenging complacency about the remaining time.

column5: Believers belong to day, not night
column6: The commentary makes remaining people a distinct group amid the alternation of night and day; Paul calls believers children of light and day, assigning the temporal images an ethical identity.

column5: Wakefulness instead of sleep
column6: The commentary develops short sleep and patient alertness across time; Paul tells the community not to sleep as others do but to keep awake and sober in view of the approaching day.

column5: Rich are to become rich in good works
column6: The commentary contrasts accumulating possessions with righteous action that endures; Paul instructs the rich to be rich in good works and generous to others.

column5: Store a foundation for the future life
column6: The commentary's accumulation motif ends at the grave unless joined to right deeds; Paul pictures generosity as storing a firm foundation for the future so that people may grasp true life.

column5: The rich fade in the midst of pursuits
column6: The commentary says acquisitive effort can consume the person's unnoticed time; James likens a rich person's fading during pursuits to a flower withered by the rising sun.

column5: Twelve hours mark the usable day
column6: The commentary treats the day as a bounded segment in which one's way matters; Jesus asks whether the day has twelve hours and connects walking without stumbling to its light.

column5: Faithful waiting through night watches
column6: The commentary puts patience across segmented night; Jesus calls servants blessed if found alert when their master comes in the second or third watch.

column5: Pray flight will not be in winter
column6: The commentary treats winter's cold as a concrete trial inside the calendar; Jesus tells hearers to pray that the expected flight not happen in winter, making season alter the hardship of endurance.

column5: Companionship sought before winter
column6: The commentary links winter's coming with people maintaining one another through time; Paul urges his addressee to come before winter, making the seasonal deadline matter for their meeting.

column5: Communal service day and night
column6: The commentary makes daily alternation part of continuing allegiance; the rescued multitude stands before God's throne and serves him day and night, extending joined devotion beyond mortal time.

column5: Separate times for scattering and gathering
column6: The commentary makes successive pieces of time carry opposing actions and later joins people; Ecclesiastes assigns separate times to scattering stones and gathering them, a concrete temporal analogy rather than an explicit claim about people.

column5: Known before formation in the womb
column6: The commentary recalls a span when the human was not yet a mentioned thing; Jeremiah's prophetic commission says God knew him before forming him in the womb, complicating any inference that pre-birth absence means divine unawareness.

column5: Afflicted yet remembers prescribed words
column6: The commentary makes endurance in truth span harsh conditions; the psalmist describes himself as a wineskin in smoke yet says he has not forgotten God's statutes, though the image is not explicitly winter cold.

column5: Tyre piles silver before its fall
column6: The commentary recalls abundance amassed before a terminal reversal; Tyre heaps silver like dust in this verse before its wealth is stripped in the next. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, with no asserted patience cognacy.

column5: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: withholding birth
column6: The table gives only a sound correspondence; God asks whether he would bring to birth and then restrain delivery, an indirect counterpart to the commentary's movement through appointed life stages and resistance to time stopping.

column5: One not yet born has not seen evil
column6: The commentary recalls a pre-existence interval in human life; Ecclesiastes calls the unborn person better off because that person has not witnessed oppression, though its judgment about nonexistence has a different purpose.

column5: Fathers and young people addressed separately
column6: The commentary names distinct stages of a life; the letter addresses fathers and young people with different spiritual descriptions, an analogy through communal age categories rather than a literal lifespan sequence.
